## Objectives

- Build a dendrogram and read it — height, merges, and where to cut
- Understand *linkage*: the one choice that changes everything, and what each option does
- Know when hierarchical beats k-means, and when it cannot be run at all
- Apply it where it fits best: grouping **patients** and **hospitals** into case-mix classes

## Why a manager cares

::: {.subtitle-frame}
Sometimes the number of groups is the question, not the input
:::

- A hospital director asks: *how many kinds of patient do we actually treat?* — k-means demands the answer before it starts
- A payer groups hospitals into peer sets for benchmarking: *which are comparable?* — and needs to see the structure at several levels, not one
- Brand managers want a tree of products, not a flat list of four segments

Hierarchical clustering gives you **all the partitions at once**, from $n$ groups down to one, and lets you choose after looking.

## [Section 1]{.section-kicker} Growing the tree {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## Agglomerative clustering, three lines

1. Start with every point as its own cluster: $n$ clusters
2. **Merge the two closest clusters**
3. Repeat until one cluster remains

$n - 1$ merges. Record the distance at each. That record *is* the dendrogram.

- Deterministic: no random starts, no seed, the same tree every time
- $k$ is not an input. You cut the tree afterwards, at any height, and read off the groups.

::: {.callout-note}
Step 2 hides the whole subject. "Closest" between two *points* is obvious. "Closest" between two *clusters* of points is a choice — the **linkage**.
:::

## Linkage: the distance between two groups

| Linkage | Distance between clusters $A$, $B$ | Produces |
|---|---|---|
| **Complete** | farthest pair: $\max_{a \in A, b \in B} d(a,b)$ | compact, similar-sized groups |
| **Single** | nearest pair: $\min d(a,b)$ | long chains; finds odd shapes, and noise |
| **Average** | mean of all pairs | a compromise, often sensible |
| **Ward** | merge that increases within-SS least | k-means-like blobs; the usual default |

Same data, four linkages, four different trees. **Ward** and **complete** are the two you will use; single is the one you should know exists so you recognise its chaining when you see it.

## By hand: five patients, one variable

::: {.subtitle-frame}
Length of stay, in days. Complete linkage.
:::

$$\{2\},\ \{3\},\ \{6\},\ \{10\},\ \{11\}$$

- Closest pair: 2 and 3 (distance 1) → $\{2,3\}$
- Next: 10 and 11 (distance 1) → $\{10,11\}$
- Now $\{2,3\}$, $\{6\}$, $\{10,11\}$. Complete linkage: $d(\{2,3\},\{6\}) = 4$, $d(\{6\},\{10,11\}) = 5$ → merge $\{2,3,6\}$ at height **4**
- Last merge at height $11 - 2 = $ **9**

Cut the tree at height 5 → two groups: *short stays* $\{2,3,6\}$ and *long stays* $\{10,11\}$. Cut at 2 → three groups. Same tree, different question.

## Reading a dendrogram

- **Leaves** are observations; **height** of a merge is the distance at which it happened
- Two leaves that merge low are similar. Two that merge only at the top are not — *even if they are drawn side by side*
- **Horizontal position carries no information.** Any subtree can be flipped. Nearness along the bottom axis means nothing.
- A long vertical gap before a merge is a natural place to cut: the groups below were far apart

::: {.callout-important title="Attention"}
The most common misreading is the third bullet. Students — and consultants — see two leaves next to each other and call them similar. Look at the height they join at, nothing else.
:::

## [Section 2]{.section-kicker} Choosing and using {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## Hierarchical or k-means?

| | k-means | Hierarchical |
|---|---|---|
| $k$ | needed in advance | chosen after seeing the tree |
| Result | one partition | every partition, nested |
| Randomness | yes — `nstart` | none |
| Scale | millions of rows | $n^2$ distances: a few thousand rows, then it stops |
| Shape | round blobs | depends on linkage |

Rule of practice: **hierarchical to explore and decide $k$; k-means to deploy at scale** with that $k$. They are colleagues, not rivals.

## In R

```{.r code-line-numbers="1-2|4|6|8-9|11"}
library(tidyverse); library(factoextra)
X <- scale(USArrests)

d  <- dist(X)                               # Euclidean, on scaled data

hc <- hclust(d, method = "ward.D2")         # or "complete", "average"

fviz_dend(hc, k = 4, rect = TRUE)           # the tree, cut at 4
groups <- cutree(hc, k = 4)                 # group label per row

table(groups)
```

::: {.callout-note}
`ward.D2` is Ward's method on Euclidean distance as Ward defined it. Plain `ward.D` squares nothing and is there for backward compatibility. Use `ward.D2`.
:::

## Patients into case-mix groups

::: {.subtitle-frame}
The application where this method earns its keep
:::

- Rows: admissions. Columns: length of stay, number of procedures, comorbidity count, ICU hours, cost
- Scale, Ward, dendrogram. The tree typically shows a clear top split — *simple* vs *complex* stays — and then a fan of subgroups
- Cut at the level clinicians recognise: they will tell you whether "four" or "seven" matches the wards they actually run
- The groups become **the units of cost accounting and benchmarking**. This is, in outline, how DRG systems were born.

::: {.callout-important title="Attention"}
Cost dominates everything if you do not scale it. And a cluster with three patients is not a case-mix group; it is three outliers. Check group sizes before you name them.
:::

## The tree is not the answer. The cut is.  {.statement}

[And the cut is a decision you defend with the height it was made at.]{.muted}
